stem: A 64-year-old suddenly loses painless vision in one eye. Fundoscopy shows a pale retina with a cherry-red fovea; there is no retinal detachment.
ask: Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Arrange immediate stroke and ophthalmology assessment for retinal arterial occlusion.
Treat as conjunctivitis with drops and review when eye pain develops.
Prescribe eye exercises and recommend gradual visual rehabilitation.
Reassure because painless loss of vision excludes ocular vascular injury.
Refer to a routine optometry appointment in four to six weeks.
explanations: A pale retina and cherry-red fovea with sudden monocular painless vision loss is typical of CRAO—an ocular stroke. Activate urgent ophthalmology/stroke assessment, vascular risk workup and check for giant cell arteritis when relevant.
Conjunctivitis causes irritation, redness and discharge, not sudden profound monocular vision loss with a cherry-red retinal spot. Drops will not restore retinal arterial perfusion.
Eye exercises cannot reopen an occluded retinal artery, and delay forfeits any time-sensitive specialist treatment and secondary stroke prevention.
Absence of pain is common in retinal artery occlusion. Acute vascular eye disease is still an emergency because retinal ischaemia can be irreversible.
Routine optometry in weeks is inappropriate. CRAO requires urgent emergency stroke/ophthalmology services and embolic or vasculitic cause assessment.
pearl: CRAO is an eye stroke; evaluate embolic sources and giant cell arteritis when relevant.
pivot: Flashes and a curtain-like field defect instead suggest retinal detachment.
